Mrs. Otis further assures me—and she is, I may observe, an authority upon Art of no small standing, having enjoyed several winters in Boston during her girlhood—that these stones possess considerable financial value and would command a handsome sum if sold. In these circumstances, Lord Canterville, you will surely understand that I cannot possibly permit them to stay in the hands of any person in my family. Indeed, such idle ornaments and baubles, however appropriate or essential to the grandeur of the British nobility, would be entirely misplaced among people reared upon the austere and, I trust, everlasting principles of republican simplicity. I ought perhaps to add that Virginia is most desirous of your permission to keep the casket in remembrance of your unhappy, though erring, forefather. Since it is exceedingly ancient, and therefore in rather poor repair, you may consider granting her wish. Personally, I must admit to considerable astonishment that a child of mine should show any sympathy whatever with mediævalism; I can explain it only by remembering that Virginia was born in a London suburb soon after Mrs. Otis returned from visiting Athens.”

Lord Canterville attended to the excellent Minister's remarks with profound gravity, occasionally tugging his grey moustache to conceal an irrepressible smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he warmly grasped his hand and replied, “My dear sir, your delightful young daughter has performed a very great service for my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, and my family and I owe her much for her astonishing bravery and spirit. The jewels are unquestionably hers; and, egad, were I cruel enough to deprive her of them, I fancy the wicked old gentleman would leave his grave within a fortnight and make my life a misery. As to their being heirlooms, an object is no heirloom unless a will or legal instrument describes it as such, and nobody has known of these jewels' existence. I promise you my claim upon them is no greater than your butler's. When Miss Virginia is older, I suspect she will enjoy possessing beautiful things to wear. Moreover, Mr. Otis, you forget that you bought both the furniture and the ghost at their assessed value. Whatever the ghost owned accordingly became yours at once; for however energetically Sir Simon may have behaved in the corridor after dark, legally he was quite dead, and his belongings passed to you through purchase.”

Week followed week, and my absorption in you continually deepened. Then something new occurred. I had depicted you as Paris in delicate armour, and as Adonis bearing a huntsman's cloak and a shining boar-spear. With a crown of heavy lotus flowers you had seated yourself in the prow of Adrian's barge, looking over the green, clouded waters of the Nile. You had bent above a motionless pool in a Greek forest, beholding the wonder of your face in its noiseless silver. All this had been what art ought to be—unselfconscious, idealised, distant. One day—a disastrous day, I sometimes feel—I decided to make a magnificent portrait of you exactly as you are, wearing your own clothes in your own age, rather than the dress of vanished centuries. I cannot say whether it was the realism of my approach, or simply the marvel of your personality presented so immediately, without haze or covering. Yet I do know that while I painted, each thin layer and particle of pigment appeared to expose my secret. I began to fear that other people would discover my worship of you. Dorian, I felt I had disclosed too much, had allowed too much of myself to enter the canvas. That was when I decided the painting must never be exhibited. You were somewhat vexed, but you did not then understand everything it signified for me. Harry laughed when I spoke to him about it. That did not trouble me. After I had completed the portrait and sat alone before it, I knew my decision was right.... Well, within a few days it departed from the studio, and once I escaped the unbearable spell of its presence, I began to think myself foolish for imagining it revealed anything beyond your extraordinary good looks and my ability to paint. Even now I cannot avoid the feeling that we err in supposing the passion experienced while creating is actually visible in the finished creation. Art remains more abstract than we imagine. Shape and colour speak only of shape and colour—nothing else. Often I think art hides its maker much more thoroughly than it discloses him. Thus, when the invitation from Paris arrived, I resolved to give your portrait the chief place in my exhibition. I never imagined you might decline. Now I understand that you were right. We cannot exhibit the picture. You must not resent me, Dorian, for what I have confided to you.

Raymond drew fresh energy from the intense pleasure of recovering his health. As general of the Athenians, he felt he held a position equal to his ambitions. In anticipating the conquest of Constantinople, he envisioned an event that would stand as a landmark across the emptiness of the ages, a feat without parallel in human history. This city, rich in historical associations and renowned throughout the world for the beauty of its setting, had been a Muslim stronghold for centuries. Now it would be rescued from slavery and barbarism and restored to a people celebrated for their genius, civilization, and love of freedom. Perdita settled into his renewed companionship, his love, his hopes, and his fame as a lover of luxury might recline on a sumptuous couch. Every thought brought rapture; every emotion seemed immersed in a warm and soothing element.

We reached Kishan on July 7. Throughout the journey the weather had been peaceful. Each morning we left our camp before dawn and watched the darkness withdraw from the hills and valleys before the golden splendor of the approaching sun. With their country's characteristic liveliness, the soldiers accompanying us delighted enthusiastically in the beauty of nature. They greeted the rising sun with triumphant music, while fragments of birdsong filled the pauses. At midday we set up our tents in a shaded valley or beneath the shelter of a mountain wood, where a stream murmuring over stones lulled us into welcome sleep. Our evening march was quieter, yet even more delightful than the restless excitement of the morning. When the band played, its members instinctively chose melodies of restrained emotion. A lover's farewell or lament for an absent beloved would give way to a solemn hymn, bringing the music to a close in harmony with the evening's peaceful beauty and lifting the soul toward lofty, religious thoughts. Often every sound ceased so that we could hear the nightingale, while fireflies danced in shining rhythms and the soft call of the aziolo promised the travelers fine weather. Whenever we passed through a valley, gentle shadows and beautifully colored rocks surrounded us. From a mountain, Greece unfolded below like a living map, its famous peaks cutting into the sky, its rivers tracing silver threads through fertile ground. We English travelers gazed in ecstasy, almost afraid to breathe, at scenery so different from the muted colors and melancholy beauty of our homeland. After we left Macedonia, the rich but low-lying plains of Thrace offered fewer lovely sights; still, the journey remained absorbing. An advance guard announced our arrival, and the country people quickly set about honoring Lord Raymond.
